chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Keeping a book of available musicians, and the value of a steady personnel
summary: Following Jimmie Lunceford's book of 3,000 players, Horace noted each man's reading and improvising ability and still values keeping the same personnel together.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yeah, he had a reporter, but I would come back and rave about certain musicians, you know, that weren't working, and I'd keep my little book with me, you know, and like the great Jimmie Lunceford always carried a book. Man, he had a book full of saxophone players, trombone -- had over 3,000 guys in there, so if he ever needed anybody, you know, he could get them. This is where I picked that up, you know, so I began to do it, and I found out it came in handy, because you never know. Maybe a guy might give you a notice, and he might be a great musician, you know, in your band, one of those things, and you wouldn't feel it as much if you knew that you had the address of the guy, and you'd always write whether he was good or fair or excellent, you know, and what his potential was and --
Whether he could read or not.

-- whether he could read, or whether he was a great ad lib man. You'd write all this by the name. This way it was like a dictionary, and it was a great thing to have. In fact, right today I do the same thing, you know. I don't have as much trouble because I've been fortunate enough to keep the personnel the same, which means a lot, you know,, because, as you know and I know, the more you keep the same personnel together, the guys know exactly what the other guy's going to do. That way you get so you can play real, real good blend
